title: Aggregates and invariants
idea: An aggregate is a cluster of objects changed as one unit through a single root entity, which guards the invariants: rules that must always hold.

analogy.text: A bank teller is the only way into your account. You never open the vault to move cash yourself, so every rule gets checked.
analogy.breaks: Tellers can bend rules; a root never lets an invariant break.

points: Outsiders hold only the root; inner parts are reached through its methods.
The root checks every invariant before changing state, so bad changes never land.
Reference other aggregates by id, not object, so each stays small and loads alone.
Keep aggregates small; save one aggregate per transaction, as DDD guidance suggests.

steps.caption: `PurchaseOrder` and its lines form one aggregate. The root is the only object outsiders may hold.
A caller wants a new line. It asks the root; it never touches the list.
The root builds the proposed list and hands it to one private gate.
The gate checks the budget and the status. On failure it throws and the old lines stay intact.
Going round the root fails: lines are immutable records, and `lines()` returns a copy.
The supplier is a separate aggregate. The order keeps only its id, so loading one never loads both.
A repository loads and saves the whole aggregate through its root. Next page covers repositories.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: The budget rule is checked in one method, but two side doors skip it.

walk.text: `OrderLine` has a mutable `quantity` field. Any holder can change it.
The budget invariant is checked only inside `addLine`.
`lines()` returns the live list, so callers can add lines without the check.
Two callers use the side doors: one appends a line, one doubles a quantity.
The order now breaks its own rule. Nothing threw; the data is simply wrong.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: One root, immutable parts, one gate for every invariant. Rejected changes leave no trace.

walk.text: `OrderLine` is an immutable record. A quantity change creates a new line.
The supplier is held by id only. The other aggregate stays out of this boundary.
Every change builds a proposed list first; the real list is untouched so far.
`commit` checks status and budget, then swaps in the new lines. All or nothing.
The getter returns a copy, closing the side door from the problem code.
Three bad changes are rejected, and the order still holds one valid line.

pitfalls: Returning the live inner list lets callers bypass the root; return `List.copyOf` instead.
Holding another aggregate by reference can drag it into every load; store its id.
Checking invariants in a service instead of the root lets a second service skip them.

quiz.q: An `Order` must never have more than 10 lines. Where should that check live?
options: In the Order root's method that adds a line
In the controller before calling addLine
quiz.why: The rule spans all lines, so only the root sees them all. A controller check is skipped by other callers, and one `OrderLine` cannot count its siblings.

takeaway: Change an aggregate only through its root, which keeps every invariant true.

starters: How do I decide where one aggregate ends and another begins?
How do I keep a rule that spans two aggregates consistent?
Should the root throw checked or unchecked exceptions for broken invariants?
